posts.body_html: Just wondering if there's any updated consensus or altered opinions on this. I've got a lot of S. leucophylla (too many honestly, but that's what happens when you grow from seed) and I didn't get good fall pitchers from them last year. In the spring I tried to spread them out more but they're still too close together. I'm starting to see quite a few diminutive pitchers with big alas as well as plain phyllodia. My thought was to just thin out their leaves, mostly cutting out the oldest ones, but after reading through this again I decided to also remove any phyllodia-like leaves. Good idea or bad idea? I'm in the hottest part of Los Angeles and although it didn't really clear up and warm up until the beginning of July, we're close to 100f now and high temps can last through September. And what about S. x readii? Similar thinking?

Having tried removing phyllodia I would strongly recommend against it. It produced the worst fall season for leucophylla I've had in my time seriously growing. My best results come from spreading out the plants as much as possible without removing any green foliage. If I cram everything together I can get all of my leucophylla in 2 big tubs. About a month ago I spread them out into 3 tubs (50% more room for everyone) to give them all more space in advance of their fall push. I'm optimistic I'll have a good fall season with them having more space.

posts.body_html:
strongly agree with D(anny)powell, don't remove the phyllodia! If the plants are already crammed and there's no chance of spacing them, the best you can do is trim ONLY the tops of the old summer traps maybe a week or two before the fall traps emerge. It sometimes opens up just enough extra light to get those fall traps going! Remove unpollinated flower stalks as well, that does help a little bit.

With regards to trimming summer traps, Only trim off the top portion of the trap that is browning or looks like it will brown up soon. Do not trim the any summer traps "below the insect line" aka don't cut out the part of the trap that is stuffed with insects, keep that in tact! That's key to getting large fall traps, those smaller summer traps full of insects are the reason the plant has energy to produce a large show of fall traps! You can cut off the trap's "head", which will prevent the trap from catching more insects, but leave the rest on to feed the fall traps.

posts.body_html: I find it's a good idea to really reduce the watering in September so that you keep the soil temperature as high as possible. Chilly nights and a high water table can depress temperatures in the pot. Also only refill the water in the morning so that the sun can warm it up during the day.
